Our algorithm is straightforward; we should compute the integer value of wg1such that Equation (5) holds. We note that Equation (5)may not hold for an integer value of wg1. In this case the goal is to compute the integer value of wg1such that the left side of Equation (5)is as close as possible to the right side of Equation (5). A naive implementation is to try every value of wg1and calculate the value of the left and right side of Equation (5)by simply evaluate every term in the sum. Such an implementation would take Ω(n3)time because we should try O(n) values ofwg1, and for each such value the calculation of each side of Equation (5)takesΩ(n2)time to evaluate the summations. We first show an exact near-linear time algorithm to compute the value of wg1that solves Equation 5 and then we briefly discuss an approximation algorithm that is used in our experiments to efficiently evaluate the sums of the binomial function. Efficient exact computation.We first assume that we have two groups, the unpopular elements g1and the popular elements g2. Then we extend our method to multiple groups G={ g1,..., gl}. Similarly, to the previous section, let E(n g1,d,w g1)be the function that represents the left side of Equation 5. Equivalently, the right side of Equation (5)is captured byE(n g2,d,w−w g1). By definition, the function Ecomputes the expected error of group g1(resp. g2) elements. The values ng1,ng2, anddare fixed, so the more bins allocated to group g1(respectively, g2) elements, the smaller the expected error. Hence, the function E(n g1,d,w g1)is monotone decreasing with respect towg1, whileE(n g2,d,w−w g1)is monotone increasing with respect to wg1. We formally establish the monotonicity ofEin the following proposition. The proof is shown in Appendix B. Proposition 1.For fixednandd, the functionE(n,d,w)is decreasing with respect tow. This property leads to the observation that instead of trying all values of wg1, we can run a binary search in the range [1,...,n] and compute the best value of wg1. The overall idea of our algorithm is the following. For every value of wg1in the binary search, we evaluate E(n g1,d,w g1) andE(n g2,d,w−w g1). IfE(n g1,d,w g1)<E(n g2,d,w−w g1)then we try larger values of wg1in the binary search. Otherwise, we continue the binary search with smaller values. In the end, we return the value of wg1found by the binary search such that |E(n g1,d,w g1)−E(n g2,d,w−w g1)|is minimized. Even if someone naively applies binary search, the running time would be Ω(n2)to evaluate the sums. Improving fairness usually comes at a cost, known as the “price of fairness” (aka cost of fairness) – the reduction in the overall performance as a result of resolving unfairness [ 15]. After introducing FCM and its details, in this section, we study its price of fairness. Following Equation 1, the overall performance of a CM sketch can be measured in terms of the sum of its expected additive error across all element typesU={e 1,···,en}. While this partition is the same as the one we used in our analysis, our objective is orthogonal to their problem. They do not necessarily aim to achieve the same estimation error between low and high frequency elements. Instead, they process light and heavy elements separately trying to improve the overall estimation error. To the best of our knowledge, none of these traditional and learned schemes can handle fair count-min estimations with theoretical guarantees. Finally, learning has been used to obtain other data structures as well, such asB-trees [54] or bloom filters [54, 62, 86]. Fairness.Fairness in data-driven systems has been studied by various research communities but mostly in machine learning (ML) [ 14,60,67]. Most of the existing work is on training a ML model that satisfies some fairness constraints. Some pioneering fair-ML efforts include [ 20,21,36,39,46,52,88]. Biases in data has also been studied extensively [ 9,10,66,73,77,83] to ensure data has been prepared responsibly [ 64,74,75,79]. Recent studies of fair algorithm design include fair clustering [ 3,16,18, 24,25,49,57,76], fairness in resource allocation and facility location problem [ 17,34,42,47,51,93], min cut [ 55], max cover [ 7], set cover [ 30], game theoretic approaches [ 4,35,92], hiring [ 6,70], ranking [8, 80, 81, 89], recommendation [23, 56, 84], representation learning [48], etc. Fairness in data structures is significantly under-studied, with the existing work being limited to [11–13,78]. Aumuller et al. [ 11–13] study individual fairness in near-neighbor search, while to the best of our knowledge, Shahbazi et al. [ 78] is the only work that studies group fairness in data structure design, and more specifically in hashing. Both in nearest-neighbor search and fair hashing, the objective is fundamentally different, so these techniques cannot be used for our FCM sketch.

CM sketches have a wide range of range of applications including heavy hitters detection to detecting rare words (infrequent items that are not stop-word) in NLP settings [44], to AQP [28]. Still, identifying heavy hitters is known as one of the traditional applications of CM sketches. For heavy hitters detection, FCM performs equally to the standard CM. A heavy hitter in the standard sketch remains a heavy hitter in FCM. This is because CM sketches, including FCM, alwaysoverestimate the frequencies. As a result, FCMnever missesa heavy hitter due to its fairness mechanism.
